title: Bagoré Bathily's Bet on Milk That Senegal's Dairies Ignored
dek: In 2006 a young vet built a dairy at Richard Toll to buy fresh milk from Fulani herders, in a market that ran on imported powder.

story.event: Founding a dairy that buys fresh milk daily from Fulani herders around Richard Toll instead of using imported powder
story.summary: In 2006 Bagoré Bathily, a Franco-Senegalese veterinarian, founded La Laiterie du Berger at Richard Toll in northern Senegal to buy fresh milk daily from Fulani herders, in a market where most milk was reconstituted from imported powder. Starting with about 200 herders supplying numbered churns on trust, the dairy faced low yields, dry-season shortages, late paydays and taxes that favoured powder; it blended much of its fresh milk with powder to meet demand and expected to balance its books for the first time only in 2016.
paragraphs: In the mid-2000s Bagoré Bathily, a Franco-Senegalese vet born in Dakar and trained in Belgium, started from one observation: by his count, 90 per cent of the milk sold in Senegal was imported, mostly as powder, in a country where cattle supported about 30 per cent of the population. Around Richard Toll, near the Mauritanian border, Fulani herders had milk and skills but, he later told the Guardian, “nobody was buying what they had to sell.”

He decided to build a dairy that would buy their fresh milk every day. With no business training, he spent a hard year writing the plan alone at home with his newborn daughter. The conditions were discouraging. The herders' cows gave on average 0.7 litres a day, Jeune Afrique reported; milk dried up in the dry season, when many families moved their herds south; there were few roads; and fresh milk soured fast in the heat. Every other dairy reconstituted imported powder. He founded La Laiterie du Berger at Richard Toll in 2006 and raised about 700 million CFA francs ($1.1 million).

The system ran on trust, not contracts. Collectors drove bush tracks morning and evening; each supplier had a numbered churn and was paid in cash at the end of the month. About 200 herders supplied it at first. In the dry season the dairy sold them feed against their milk payments, so fewer had to migrate. A 2012 field survey found payday often late because of cash-flow problems, the herders' main complaint.

The bet paid slowly. Revenue rose from 250 million CFA francs in the first year to 1.4 billion in 2011; Bathily said he needed about 3 billion to break even. To keep up with demand, the Guardian reported in 2016, the dairy mixed most of its fresh milk with powder, while taxes on collecting local milk came to about 30 per cent against 7 per cent on imported powder. That year was the first in which he expected to balance the books.

“Had I known it would have taken this long to make this amount of money, I would have stopped,” he told the Christian Science Monitor in 2017. His herders, he said, now earned two or three times what they had before.

quote.text: Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is. If you say to me now that you want a fig, I will answer to you that it requires time: let it flower first, then put forth fruit, and then ripen.
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Epictetus told an impatient questioner that nothing great arrives suddenly, not even a fig. Bathily's dairy took about ten years to reach the point where it expected to balance its books, and the herders' trust had to flower first, one paid month at a time.

reflection: Bathily's line about stopping deserves to be taken seriously rather than as a joke. Not knowing how long it would take was part of what let him begin. Knowing it would not have made the cows give more milk or the tracks any shorter.

Some of your work runs on the same slow clock: trust that builds with each month you keep your word, skills that ripen with repetition, people who come round in their own time. On days when progress feels invisible, it may help to judge the season you are in rather than the harvest you hoped to have by now.
invitation: Pick one slow thing you are building. Write down one sign, however small, that it has grown since this time last year, and leave the rest of the question for another day.

cross_checks.claim: La Laiterie du Berger was founded at Richard Toll in 2006 (the CSM says it opened in 2007)
Most milk sold in Senegal was imported or reconstituted from imported powder
About 200 herders supplied the dairy at the start
The decision: to buy fresh milk directly from Fulani herders when other dairies used powder
The dairy took years to approach break-even (needing about 3 billion CFA francs of revenue; expecting to balance its books in 2016)

research_notes: Founding year: the 2012 field survey and the Guardian (2016) say 2006; the Christian Science Monitor (2017) says Bathily spent a year on the plan and another 12 months building the factory and 'opened' the company in 2007; a search summary also turned up 2005. The story uses 2006 for the founding, as both the survey and the Guardian do, and notes the CSM's 2007 in cross_checks. Supplier numbers: about 200 at the start (survey and CSM agree); the survey gives almost 800 in 2010, the CSM a peak of 800 in June 2016 and about 500 families, the Guardian about 300 families reached by collectors; the story gives only the starting figure. Price: FCFA 200 a litre unchanged since 2006 (survey, 2012) and 225 (CSM, 2017); not used. Collection radius: 50 km (survey), 'an area of 32km' (Guardian); the story avoids a figure. Powder: the Guardian (2016) says the dairy mixed most of its fresh milk with powder to meet demand and sold a premium line made only with Senegalese milk; the CSM (2017) says Dolima products would 'have to be made with powdered milk' if collection stopped, which implies a blend rather than all-powder; the story gives the Guardian's account with attribution. Funding: 700 million CFA francs raised at the start (CSM); Danone-linked funds held 45% by 2016 (Guardian); set to 'mixed'. The 0.7 litres a day yield and the revenue figures come from a 2012 Jeune Afrique article reprinted on au-senegal.com (the original Jeune Afrique URL no longer loads); they are the company's figures as reported. Earnings 'two or three times' before is Bathily's own estimate to the CSM. The CSM also reports a VAT dispute in 2017 that led the dairy to cut its herder pool by nearly half; that falls after this episode and is left out. Epictetus's reply concerns a man asking how to stop his brother being angry; it is applied by analogy.
